grammar.title: Gramatyka
grammar.rule: My pracujemy. Wy pracujecie. Ludzie pracują. Grupa pracuje. Każdy pracuje.
grammar.note_en:
A plural verb agrees with a plural subject. The subject tells us who does it. My pracujemy means “we work”; wy pracujecie means “you work”, addressing more than one person; ludzie pracują means “people work”. My includes the speaker. Wy identifies the group being addressed. When Ala says my about the chair task, she includes herself; when Irena addresses that working group, she uses wy. A named group such as Ala i Jan takes the third-person plural: Ala i Jan pracują, “Ala and Jan work”. The present forms of być were met earlier; this chapter adds plural action verbs.

Learn the three actual forms for each verb. Pracujemy/pracujecie/pracują mean “we work/you work/they work”. Pomagamy/pomagacie/pomagają mean “we help/you help/they help”. Robimy/robicie/robią mean “we do/you do/they do”. Nosimy/nosicie/noszą mean “we carry/you carry/they carry”. Sprzątamy/sprzątacie/sprzątają mean “we clean or tidy/you clean or tidy/they clean or tidy”. Polish often leaves my or wy unspoken because the verb ending identifies the person. The first-person plural forms here end in -my and the second-person plural forms in -cie. Learn the third-person forms as whole words: pracują, pomagają, robią, noszą, sprzątają. Do not build every third-person plural by adding the same letters to its citation form.

These present endings do not change with the workers’ gender. Ala i Ewa sprzątają means “Ala and Ewa clean”; Ala i Jan noszą krzesła means “Ala and Jan carry chairs”. The all-female pair and the mixed pair both use third-person plural action forms. A noun’s masculine-personal plural classification is a separate issue; it does not create different present-tense verb endings for male and female workers. No past tense is being taught here.

A collective noun names a group as one grammatical unit. Grupa means “group” and is singular: Grupa pracuje, “The group works”. Ludzie means “people” and is plural: Ludzie pracują, “People work”. The same actual adults can be viewed as one group or as several people. Grupa pracują is not the demonstrated agreement. Każdy means “each” or “everyone”, considering the individuals one at a time. Każdy pracuje means “Everyone works”, with a singular verb. It does not mean that each person must perform the same job: Irena can support the table while someone carries and someone else cleans.

Człowiek means “person” or “human being”; it can identify an adult of either sex. Its usual plural is ludzie, “people”, an irregular pair to learn together. This chapter uses both as naming forms and subjects. It does not teach personal direct objects or other human cases. Nauczyciele means “teachers”, and uczniowie means “learners/students”. In a group containing Jan and Ala, uczniowie is the masculine-personal nominative plural even though Ala is a woman. The naming frame Tu są uczniowie means “Here are learners”. It is not a plural instrumental predicate. These noun spellings are individual demonstrated forms, not a rule that every person noun ends the same way.

Keep occupation and task role distinct. Jan remains a teacher by occupation and a learner in the practical task. Irena remains a carpenter and is the temporary instructor here. Nauczyciele can group Jan in his stated occupation with Irena in that local teaching role; it does not give Irena a new permanent profession. Uczniowie identifies Ala and Jan in the task. The English reference does not turn these labels into claims about school enrolment or institutions.

Pomagać is used without a recipient object here. Pomagamy means “We help”, supported by the known noun pomoc, “help”, and by actual complementary work. Who receives help would require a construction not taught here. Robić is the general verb “do/make”: Co robisz? is “What are you doing?” and Robię rysunek is “I am making a drawing”. Co robimy? asks “What are we doing?” The answer can name the actual activity, such as Nosimy krzesła, “We carry chairs”, or Sprzątamy, “We are cleaning”.

Nosić describes the carrying task, handling chairs within the workshop. Noszą krzesła is “They carry chairs”. It does not introduce a specified journey, direction, source, or the distinct verb for carrying something in one direction. Sprzątać covers cleaning and tidying: one person uses the szczotka, “brush”, while another clears a chair from the floor area. Wejście means “entrance”. Clearing the chair changes the available passage; a guest’s large bag and the small entrance keep the access problem concrete without diagnosing the guest or narrating travel.

The chapter retains positive plural objects such as krzesła, “chairs”, learned earlier. It does not teach plural genitive objects under negation, plural oblique cases, personal direct objects, recipients or ownership genitives. A sentence such as Tu nie ma krzesła, “There is no chair here”, uses the already known singular genitive krzesła. The identically spelled positive plural krzesła in Nosimy krzesła has a different grammatical job. Context, not spelling alone, tells you which use is intended.

The SMS headed Pomoc is distinct from the workshop owner’s visit plan. The new outgoing reply belongs to Ewa and the workshop group; it reports their present work. It does not identify the unseen senders, promise an arrival or establish ownership of the lamp, tool or bag. The newly observed guest is not identified as the workshop owner or a member of the SMS group.
